title: SQL SELECT Fundamentals

steps.title: Read data with SELECT
steps.content: SELECT specifies the columns to return. FROM specifies the table. SQL reads the requested rows and columns; it does not change the stored table.
steps.example: SELECT name, marks FROM Student; returns only name and marks for every student.
steps.tip: Use explicit column names in production queries instead of SELECT * when you know the required fields.

steps.title: Filter rows
steps.prompt: Which clause filters rows where marks are at least 70?
steps.explanation: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping or final ordering.
hints: Identify which SQL clause performs the task in the question.
Separate selecting columns, filtering rows, grouping rows and sorting results.

steps.title: Sort and limit results
steps.content: ORDER BY sorts returned rows. ASC is ascending and DESC is descending. In SQL dialects that support it, FETCH FIRST or LIMIT can restrict the number of rows.
steps.example: SELECT name, marks FROM Student ORDER BY marks DESC; puts the highest marks first.

steps.title: Find the top score
steps.prompt: Which query returns students with marks greater than 80, highest marks first?
options: SELECT * FROM Student WHERE marks > 80 ORDER BY marks DESC;
SELECT * FROM Student ORDER BY marks > 80;
SELECT * FROM Student GROUP BY marks > 80;
steps.explanation: WHERE selects rows with marks > 80. ORDER BY marks DESC sorts them from highest to lowest.
hints: Identify which SQL clause performs the task in the question.
Separate selecting columns, filtering rows, grouping rows and sorting results.

steps.title: Aggregate functions
steps.content: COUNT counts rows or non-NULL values; SUM adds values; AVG calculates the mean; MIN and MAX return extremes. GROUP BY creates a separate result group for each key.
steps.example: SELECT department, AVG(salary) FROM Employee GROUP BY department; calculates an average for each department.

steps.title: Write a filtered and sorted query
steps.content: The Student table stores one row per learner. Use SELECT to choose columns, WHERE to filter rows and ORDER BY to sort the result. The grading data stays on the server; only the schema and sample rows are shown here.
steps.prompt: Return each student's name and marks where marks are at least 80, sorted from highest marks to lowest.
steps.schema_preview: Student(id INTEGER, name TEXT, marks INTEGER, department TEXT)
steps.sample_data:
id | name | marks | department
1 | Asha | 92 | CSE
2 | Ravi | 76 | ECE
3 | Mira | 85 | CSE
4 | Dev | 68 | MECH
steps.schema_ddl: CREATE TABLE Student (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, marks INTEGER NOT NULL, department TEXT NOT NULL);
steps.seed_inserts: INSERT INTO Student VALUES (1, 'Asha', 92, 'CSE'); INSERT INTO Student VALUES (2, 'Ravi', 76, 'ECE'); INSERT INTO Student VALUES (3, 'Mira', 85, 'CSE'); INSERT INTO Student VALUES (4, 'Dev', 68, 'MECH');
steps.expected_query: SELECT name, marks FROM Student WHERE marks >= 80 ORDER BY marks DESC;
steps.explanation: WHERE keeps Asha and Mira because their marks are at least 80. ORDER BY marks DESC places Asha (92) before Mira (85).
hints: First choose only the columns requested: name and marks.
Filter the rows with WHERE marks >= 80.
Sort the remaining rows with ORDER BY marks DESC.

steps.title: Understand the query pipeline
steps.content: A query is written in a familiar clause order. Its logical processing order starts with FROM, then WHERE, then SELECT; ORDER BY is applied to the result.
steps.prompt: Arrange the logical steps for a simple filtered SELECT query.
options: Sort the final result with ORDER BY
steps.explanation: FROM provides the source rows, WHERE filters them, SELECT projects requested columns, and ORDER BY sorts the result.
hints: The database needs a source table before it can filter rows.
Filtering happens before the final output columns are selected in the logical query-processing model.

steps.title: Repair a WHERE and ORDER BY mix-up
steps.content: The analyst wants students with marks above 80, highest first. The query sorts by a Boolean comparison instead of filtering rows.
options: Add WHERE marks > 80 before ORDER BY marks DESC

feedback_by_option.1: The query still needs SELECT for the requested columns and FROM for the table. WHERE is a separate filtering clause.
feedback_by_option.2: GROUP BY is used for aggregation; it does not replace a row filter.
feedback_by_option.3: Without FROM, the query has no Student table source.

steps.explanation: Use WHERE marks > 80 to filter rows, then ORDER BY marks DESC to sort the qualifying rows.
hints: Filtering and sorting are different jobs.
Use WHERE for the condition and ORDER BY for the sort direction.

questions.prompt: Which clause identifies the source table?
questions.explanation: FROM names the table or tables being queried.

questions.prompt: Which query selects only names from Student?
questions.explanation: SELECT name FROM Student is the correct basic query structure.

questions.prompt: Which clause sorts marks from highest to lowest?

questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts all rows in the result set.

questions.prompt: Which clause filters groups after aggregation?
questions.explanation: HAVING filters grouped results; WHERE filters rows before grouping.

learning_objectives: Select only the columns required by a question.
Filter rows using WHERE and comparison operators.
Sort rows using ORDER BY ASC and DESC.
Explain the distinction between row filtering and grouping.
Write and validate a read-only SELECT query.

common_misconceptions.correction: WHERE filters rows; ORDER BY sorts the rows that remain.

common_misconceptions.misconception: GROUP BY is another way to sort rows.
common_misconceptions.correction: GROUP BY forms groups for aggregation; ORDER BY sorts the final result.

common_misconceptions.misconception: SELECT * is always the best choice.
common_misconceptions.correction: Selecting only required columns makes queries clearer and can reduce unnecessary data transfer.

worked_examples.title: Select columns
worked_examples.explanation: SELECT names the columns to include; FROM names the source table.

worked_examples.title: Filter rows
worked_examples.input: SELECT name FROM Student WHERE marks >= 60;
trace: Keep rows whose marks are at least 60.
Return the name for each kept row.
worked_examples.output: Names of students scoring 60 or more
worked_examples.explanation: WHERE keeps rows that satisfy its Boolean condition.

worked_examples.title: Sort the result
worked_examples.input: SELECT name, marks FROM Student ORDER BY marks DESC;
worked_examples.explanation: ORDER BY sorts the returned rows; it does not update the table.

Which SQL clause sorts returned rows?
